### Description

Therapy has always been associated with the values of Eurocentric or Western perspective. Conversely, African Americans seldom turn to therapy when attempting to deal with racial trauma in this society. Yet, this has been even more reason not to seek out the source of dealing with the racial stigmas imposed on the community. The theoretical framework of critical race theory (CRT) was the basis for studying how the issues of race and racism permeate our society in ways where they must be recognized and processed in the therapy room. This qualitative phenomenological study involved interviewing six African American trained eye movement desensitization and reprocessing (EMDR)-therapy clinicians to examine the effectiveness and the relevance of the treatment of trauma using this therapy in working with African American children. This study acknowledges the stigmas and offers recommendations to make the trauma-based model of EMDR more relatable to the African American child. Results from the analysis of the interviews with these therapists show how children are impacted by modifying what goes on in the room. This study may also serve to assist therapists across the racial divide to work and connect with African American clients who struggle with racism that is interwoven in the fabric of our society.

- Slow down and integrate titration to avoid emotional flooding.
- Offer somatic and creative processing (e.g., movement, drumming, or bilateral tapping) to make EMDR more accessible.

## Understanding Oppression As Trauma, Not Mere Context  
Historically, trauma frameworks quietly file racism and oppression under external stressors; the weather around the client rather than the wound itself. But the nervous system doesn't make that distinction. It encodes oppression as a threat. It encodes oppression as trauma.  
When we treat oppression as mere context, we target the wrong thing, and sometimes we further harm the very people we are trying to support. EMDR, done with this lens, can hold oppression-based experience as the target memory itself; but only if we adapt the protocol to a truth the standard model wasn't built for: the threat is often still present. And the threat may be externally validated.
I also write as someone having done EMDR Therapy as a client around the harmful messaging received being part of intentionally marginalized communities.
## Tending to Racial Dynamics In Therapy  
While the therapeutic relationship does build some community, the therapy relationship itself carries a racial dynamic. We can’t process someone's racial trauma “neutrally” because race is in the room. This is where the therapist must also be in community, for consultation, accountability, and supervision, as we address the inherent power dynamics (and others) of the therapeutic relationship.  
As providers, we also must be connected to our communities to know the adaptive spaces and places that may support those we serve. We must practice community to truly model community.  
EMDR is one tool. Used with respect for the realities of oppression and ongoing trauma, it becomes a way of challenging oppression; by refusing to reproduce the harm inside the therapy room.

seltz.title: Decolonizing EMDR: Centering Client Voice and Choice in Trauma Healing
seltz.snippet:
**Traditional trauma therapy has long focused on the individual—how a person processes and stores distressing experiences in the brain. But what happens when trauma is not just personal, but systemic?** What if the distress a client carries isn’t just from isolated incidents but from generations of harm, ongoing discrimination, and structural oppression?

For many clients, especially those from marginalized communities, trauma isn’t just an event—it’s a lived reality, woven into their daily experiences. Yet, traditional therapy models often treat distress as something that happens to a person, rather than something that happens within a larger system.

This is why EMDR needs to evolve. While it’s a powerful tool for trauma healing, its traditional framework doesn’t always account for systemic oppression or intergenerational trauma. Jasmine Adams, LCSW, EMDRIA Approved Consultant, has seen this firsthand.

*\"My personal experience in oppressive situations and also from my work with therapy participants who have experienced oppressions and learning ways to best support them,\"* Adams explains.
